planting.note: Direct sow in fall or plant divisions into sharply drained, constantly moist soil in full sun to light shade; Sow-Thistle Primrose needs cool summers and is genuinely difficult outside alpine-house conditions in mild or hot climates.

directions: Plant in full sun to light shade in sharply drained soil kept constantly moist through the growing season; Sow-Thistle Primrose carries large, coarse, sow-thistle-like leaves that emerge after flowering, with violet-blue, farina-dusted flower umbels on 4-8 inch stems in spring. It is native to alpine meadows of Yunnan, Sichuan, and Tibet at 3,000-4,500 meters elevation, and needs cool summers to thrive, making it a genuine challenge outside an alpine house in mild or hot climates. Source seed through alpine or rock-garden society exchanges, since live plants are rarely offered commercially.
sources: NARGS (North American Rock Garden Society) seed exchange

planting.note: Direct sow in fall or plant divisions into humus-rich, constantly moist soil in part shade; Wilson's Candelabra Primrose wants streamside or bog-garden conditions like its better-known candelabra relatives.

directions: Plant in part shade to full sun in humus-rich, constantly moist soil; Wilson's Candelabra Primrose bears whorled candelabra flowers in reddish-purple to magenta with a yellow eye on stems 12-18 inches tall, blooming late spring to early summer. It is native to moist meadows and streamsides of Yunnan and Sichuan, and needs the same streamside or bog-garden culture as its better-known candelabra cousins already in cultivation. Seed is available through specialty sources including Chiltern Seeds, Jelitto, and Plant World Seeds.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall or plant divisions into moist but well-drained, humus-rich soil in part shade; Snow Primrose prefers cool summers.

directions: Plant in part shade in moist but well-drained, humus-rich soil; Snow Primrose bears fragrant, pure white to cream flowers held in tiered, farina-dusted whorls on stems 8-16 inches tall, blooming in late spring. It is native to Himalayan and southwest Chinese alpine meadows and performs best with cool summers, making it most successful in climates without extended hot, humid stretches. Seed is available through specialty sources including Chiltern Seeds and rock-garden society exchanges.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall or plant divisions into constantly moist, humus-rich soil in part shade; Chinese Purple Primrose is a classic damp-meadow bog-garden primula.

directions: Plant in part shade in constantly moist, humus-rich soil; Chinese Purple Primrose bears violet-purple flowers in tiered whorls on farina-dusted white stems 12-24 inches tall, blooming late spring into early summer. It is native to wet alpine meadows and streambanks of Sichuan, Yunnan, and Tibet, and is a classic damp-meadow bog-garden primula best grown alongside other moisture-loving Primula species. It is carried by some UK Primula specialist nurseries, including Edrom Nurseries, in addition to specialty seed sources.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall or plant divisions into permanently moist to boggy, humus-rich soil in part shade; Involucrate Primrose is a smaller-scale companion to the already-grown Primula sikkimensis and florindae.

directions: Plant in part shade in permanently moist to boggy, humus-rich soil; Involucrate Primrose bears fragrant white, occasionally pale lilac, nodding flowers in a single umbel on short stems 4-8 inches tall, blooming late spring to early summer. It is native to wet Himalayan alpine meadows and streambanks from Kashmir to southwest China, and makes a good smaller-scale bog-garden companion to the already-grown giant Himalayan cowslip (Primula florindae) and Primula sikkimensis. It needs permanently saturated soil to thrive, more so than many other primroses.
sources: Primula specialist nurseries and seed exchanges

planting.note: Direct sow in fall or plant divisions into constantly moist to boggy, humus-rich soil in part shade; Walton's Primrose shares its culture with the already-grown Primula sikkimensis but offers a much darker flower color.

directions: Plant in part shade in constantly moist to boggy, humus-rich soil; Walton's Primrose bears deep wine-purple to maroon pendant bell flowers, farina-dusted, on stems 18-24 inches tall, blooming in early summer. It is native to wet Tibetan and Himalayan alpine meadows and shares the same moist, boggy culture as the already-grown Primula sikkimensis, but offers a notably darker flower color, making it a good contrasting companion in a bog garden's Sikkimensis-section plantings.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall or plant divisions into gritty, moisture-retentive but sharply drained soil in full sun to light shade; Modest Primrose is distinct from the already-grown Primula farinosa despite a similar farinose rosette form.

directions: Plant in full sun to light shade in gritty, moisture-retentive but sharply drained soil; Modest Primrose forms small farinose rosettes bearing pale lilac-pink to white flowers with a yellow eye on short stems 2-4 inches tall, blooming in spring. It is native to alpine rock faces and cliffs of Japan, with one variety growing on Hokkaido's coastal cliffs, and is very cold-hardy. It is a classic rock-garden farinose primula, distinct from the already-grown Primula farinosa despite the superficially similar rosette form.
sources: Japanese and alpine specialist seed sources

planting.note: Direct sow in fall into sharply drained, constantly moist soil in light to part shade with winter-wet protection; Reid's Primrose is a connoisseur's alpine, genuinely difficult to grow outside an alpine house.

directions: Plant in light to part shade in sharply drained soil kept constantly moist through the growing season, with protection from winter wet; Reid's Primrose bears fragrant pale blue-to-white pendant bell flowers, heavily dusted with farina, on short stems 2-6 inches tall, blooming in early summer. It is native to Himalayan alpine cliffs and scree in Nepal and Kashmir, and is a genuine connoisseur's alpine, notoriously hard to grow outside an alpine house and mostly obtainable only through specialty rock-garden society seed exchanges rather than retail nurseries. Only attempt it with realistic expectations about the difficulty involved.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall or plant divisions into constantly moist, gritty, humus-rich soil in part shade; Clarke's Primrose resents drying out and is among the earliest primroses to bloom.

directions: Plant in part shade (full sun only in reliably cool climates) in constantly moist, gritty, humus-rich soil; Clarke's Primrose forms tiny rosettes with bright pink, yellow-eyed flowers held almost stemless just above the foliage, one of the earliest primroses to bloom each year in very early spring. It is native to the Kashmir Himalaya and resents drying out even briefly, making it a classic small rock-garden or trough primula for a consistently moist, shaded site. It is carried by alpine specialist nurseries including Edrom and Ashwood in addition to seed sources.
